name: Cove Park
overview: Artists' residency centre at Peaton Hill, Cove, on the Rosneath Peninsula, on a 50-acre site overlooking Loch Long (Northings, 2006).
Registered as a Scottish charity on 26 October 1999 (Office of the Scottish Charity Regulator data via Find that Charity).

Named buildings: the Jacobs Building takes the founders' name. Cameron Webster Architects designed the new artists' centre, a single-storey building with two accommodation units, two studios, workshop and performance spaces, built under a £1.4 million contract awarded to Clark Contracts in November 2015 (Project Scotland).
funding_verdict: Cove Park: Creative Scotland, charitable trusts and individuals

name: Firstsite
overview: Contemporary art gallery and cinema in Lewis Gardens, High Street, Colchester CO1 1JH (Firstsite).
Established in 1993 and in its current building since 2011. The site says over 1 million visitors have come since the move (Firstsite).
Wikipedia says the building was designed by Rafael Viñoly, cost £25,542,701 to build, and that Colchester Council owns the freehold.
funding_verdict: Firstsite: mainly public with charitable trusts: Arts Council England, Colchester Borough Council and Essex County Council, plus Garfield Weston Foundation and Essex Community Foundation
wider_context: On 29 May 2026 more than 260 British artists published an open letter on the Artists for Palestine UK platform urging the National Theatre, Royal Shakespeare Company, Young Vic, Royal Court and Almeida to end partnerships with Bloomberg Philanthropies, saying the partnerships made the theatres "complicit in grave war crimes" through the foundation's involvement with illegal Israeli settlements (The New Arab, "Over 260 UK artists urge theatres to end ties with Bloomberg Philanthropies over Israel", The New Arab Staff, 29 May 2026). The letter does not name Firstsite.
The connection: Firstsite announced on 30 January 2025 that it had been selected for the Bloomberg Philanthropies Digital Accelerator programme (Firstsite).

press_items.title: Martin Bailey, "Conflict-of-interest scandal at publicly funded UK arts centre Firstsite" (20 July 2018)

name: Grizedale Arts
overview: Contemporary arts residency and commissioning agency based at Lawson Park, a hill farm above Coniston Water in the Lake District (Wikipedia, Grizedale Arts website).

Roots in the Grizedale Society, founded in 1968 by Forestry Commission head forester Bill Grant, which ran a theatre and the Grizedale Sculpture Trail. Adam Sutherland became director in 1999 and merged the Society into the new Grizedale Arts that year (Wikipedia).

Moved to Lawson Park in 2007. The farm was refurbished by Sutherland Hussey Architects as an artists' residency and office base and opened in 2009 (Wikipedia). The farm was first recorded under the ownership of Furness Abbey in the 13th century, and John Ruskin purchased the farmhouse and land in the late 19th century (Wikipedia, Lawson Park).
funding_verdict: Grizedale Arts: public support and grants: Arts Council England and South Lakeland District Council, with loan finance and donations

name: Void
overview: Contemporary art gallery at 10 Waterloo Place, Derry city centre, which it moved to in March 2021 (Void website, Open Charities).

Artists formed DADA (Derry's Artists for Derry's Art) in January 2003 to create a contemporary art space. Void Art Centre opened in January 2005 as a non-profit limited company with charitable status, with the inaugural exhibition "Peripheral Vision" (Void website).
Home was first the basement of the Old City Shirt Factory. It moved to a first-floor space there in 2015 (Void website, Photoireland wiki).
funding_verdict: Void: public and charitable funders: Arts Council of Northern Ireland, Derry City and Strabane District Council and foundations

press_items.title: Sara Greavu, "Pushback" (29 March 2017), headed "Nothing But Longing, Void Art Centre and the LD50 Gallery controversy"

name: Talbot Rice Gallery
overview: Public art gallery of the University of Edinburgh, in the Old College, South Bridge, Edinburgh EH8 9YL (Talbot Rice website).
The gallery opened in 1975. An arts centre had opened in the Quad in 1970. It is named for David Talbot Rice, the university's Watson Gordon Professor of Fine Art from 1934 to 1972 (Wikipedia).
Old College was designed by Robert Adam and completed by William Henry Playfair (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Talbot Rice Gallery: public university gallery: the University of Edinburgh, with Creative Scotland, trusts and donors for exhibitions

name: The Common Guild
overview: Visual arts organisation in Glasgow, now based at 5 Florence Street on the south bank of the River Clyde, in a former school opened in 1894 as Adelphi Terrace Public School and being developed into studios and creative businesses by Assumption Studios (stated by the space).
Founded in 2006 (Wikipedia). Katrina Brown was Founder Director and stepped down after 19 years, and Chloë Reith has been appointed Director (stated by the space).
From 2008 to 2018 it showed exhibitions at 21 Woodlands Terrace, a Victorian townhouse overlooking Kelvingrove Park (stated by the space).
funding_verdict: The Common Guild: Creative Scotland, grants and donations (stated by the space)

name: FACT
overview: Gallery and cinema centre for art and new technology at 88 Wood Street, Liverpool L1 4DQ (FACT).

FACT began as Merseyside Moviola, which screened artists' film and video in a disused chapel. Moviola founded the Video Positive festival in 1989 and in 1993 began a 10-year fundraising effort for a dedicated centre (FACT). Eddie Berg says he founded the Foundation for Art and Creative Technology in 1988 (Sculpture magazine, Robert Preece, 1 April 2004). Wikipedia names Graeme Phillips as one of the people behind it.
The building opened in 2003 as Liverpool's first new arts building in over 60 years. Wikipedia says Isaac Julien's "Baltimore" was commissioned for the opening.
funding_verdict: FACT: mainly public with charitable trusts: Arts Council England and Liverpool City Council, plus Paul Hamlyn, Jerwood, John Ellerman and Granada

name: Autograph
overview: Photography gallery and arts charity at Rivington Place, London, working on race, identity and human rights through photography.

Founded in 1988 as the Association of Black Photographers, in a small office in the Bon Marché Building in Brixton. The organisation's history page lists seven founding signatories: Monika Baker, Merle Van Den Bosch, Armet Francis, Sunil Gupta, Michael Jess, George Shire and Lance Watson. Wikipedia says the board renamed it Autograph ABP in 2002, and that Mark Sealy became director in 1991.

Rivington Place was designed by David Adjaye. It is a new-build of 1,445 square metres (Dezeen) that cost £8m (Dezeen, Building). Autograph and the Institute of New International Visual Arts (Iniva) commissioned it jointly in 2002 and it opened in October 2007, formally opened by Stuart Hall (Autograph). Building magazine's subheading calls it the first public gallery to be opened in London for 40 years.
funding_verdict: Autograph: mainly public and charitable: Arts Council England and the National Lottery Heritage Fund

name: Belarus Free Theatre
overview: Exile-run theatre company based in London, with an office at 66 The Cut, SE1 8LZ (stated by the company).

Founded in March 2005 in Minsk by Nikolai Khalezin, a playwright and journalist, and Natalia Koliada, a theatre producer. The director Vladimir Shcherban joined in May 2005. Its first production, Sarah Kane's "4.48 Psychosis", premiered on 28 May 2005 in a Minsk club (Wikipedia).
In Belarus the company had no registration or premises and performed in private apartments, cafés and forests (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Belarus Free Theatre: philanthropy and grants: private trusts, UK government and National Lottery money, and donations

name: Francis Skaryna Belarusian Library and Museum
overview: Library, archive and museum of Belarusian books, art and artefacts at 37 Holden Road in North Finchley, a short walk from Woodside Park Underground station (stated by the library).

It grew out of the Belarusian Catholic Mission, founded in London in 1947. The Mission moved to Marian House on Holden Avenue in 1948 with a collection of 200 to 300 Belarusian books brought by Fr Česlaus Sipovič (Wikipedia).
It is named for Francysk Skaryna and was called Bibliotheca Alboruthena from 1958. Robert Auty formally opened the library on 15 May 1971 (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Francis Skaryna Belarusian Library and Museum: community-funded: donations from Belarusians and friends, a small bond endowment and flat rent; no public or corporate funding

name: Mosaic Rooms
overview: Gallery and cultural space for art from the Arab region at 226 Cromwell Road, Kensington, London SW5 0SW (Mosaic Rooms website, The Art Newspaper).

Launched in November 2008 as a project of the A.M. Qattan Foundation, conceived by foundation trustee Omar al-Qattan. On 15 January 2026 the A.M. Qattan Foundation announced that it would operate as an independent organisation and a legal entity distinct from the foundation (A.M. Qattan Foundation).

Registered UK charity number 1183882. Trustees are Dr Selma Taysir Dabbagh (chair), Lamiaa Soliman (treasurer), Celeste Ricci, Maisha Akil Scafe-Smith, Dr Samaneh Moafi, Christopher Rawcliffe, Marwan Kaabour and Zainab Sahar Beyad (Mosaic Rooms website).
funding_verdict: Mosaic Rooms: private: the A.M. Qattan Foundation and the Al-Qattan Charitable Trust

name: New Art Exchange
overview: Contemporary art gallery and cultural centre in the Hyson Green neighbourhood of Nottingham, at 39-41 Gregory Boulevard, NG7 6BE (NAE website, Wikipedia).

Formed in 2003 by the merger of two grassroots groups: APNA Arts, a South Asian arts collective founded by Parbinder Singh, and East Midlands African Caribbean Arts, co-founded with educationalist and historian Len Garrison (Wikipedia).
The building was designed by Hawkins\Brown and officially opened on 5 September 2008, replacing the former Art Exchange building, previously known as The People's Dispensary (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: New Art Exchange: mainly public: Arts Council England core funding

name: Cample Line
overview: Contemporary arts organisation presenting contemporary art and film of international scope, at Cample Mill in Cample, Dumfriesshire, two miles south of Thornhill and about 14 miles north of Dumfries, overlooking the Cample rail viaduct.
Established in late 2016 and registered as a Scottish charitable incorporated organisation (SC047031) on 7 December 2016 (OSCR). Tina Fiske is Director. David Clark chairs the board.
Building: the mill was once part of a row of millworkers' cottages.
funding_verdict: Cample Line: registered Scottish charity, income £126,761 in 2025 (OSCR)

name: BAMPFA
overview: University art museum and film archive at 2155 Center Street, on the edge of the UC Berkeley campus and downtown Berkeley. Part of the University of California, Berkeley (BAMPFA site). It holds more than 25,000 artworks and 18,000 films and videos (BAMPFA site).

Founded in 1963 after the artist Hans Hofmann donated 45 paintings and $250,000. Sheldon Renan founded the Pacific Film Archive in 1967 (Wikipedia). Peter Selz was founding director. Lawrence Rinder directed from 2008 to 2020, and Julie Rodrigues Widholm has been executive director since August 2020 (Wikipedia).

Building: Diller Scofidio + Renfro rebuilt and enlarged a 1939 Art Deco printing plant, after the Mario Ciampi building of 1970 was judged seismically unsafe in 1997 and a Toyo Ito design was cancelled in 2009. The museum reopened on 31 January 2016 (Wikipedia). Wikipedia puts the cost at about $100 million. Architectural Record puts it at about $112 million.
funding_verdict: BAMPFA: university-run, with foundation and public grants
wider_context: Hollywood Foreign Press Association: BAMPFA's undated supporters page lists it in the $20,000 to $49,999 tier. Wikipedia reports that on 21 February 2021 the Los Angeles Times found none of its members was Black, and that an LA Times investigation found it regularly paid members over $1 million a year for committee service. In May 2021 Netflix and Amazon Studios paused work with it, WarnerMedia later joined them, and on 10 May 2021 NBC said it would not air the 2022 Golden Globes. Wikipedia says the association was rebranded the Golden Globe Foundation on 12 June 2023, when Dick Clark Productions and Eldridge Industries bought the Golden Globes assets.

Wikipedia reports that in 2025 about $230,000 in conservation funds from an Institute of Museum and Library Services grant was revoked by executive order, just before the "Routed West" quilt exhibition opened. The IMLS is also listed among BAMPFA's top-tier supporters.

press_items.title: Josephine Minutillo, "Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive by Diller Scofidio + Renfro" (1 March 2016)

name: Boise Art Museum
overview: Art museum at 670 Julia Davis Drive in Boise, Idaho, in Julia Davis Park (Wikipedia, museum website).

The Boise Art Association was founded on 8 October 1931. The museum opened in 1937 as the Boise Gallery of Art, a partnership between the Association, the City of Boise and the Works Progress Administration, and was renamed the Boise Art Museum in 1988 (Wikipedia).

Building: the original Art Deco and Egyptian Revival building was designed by Tourtellotte & Hummel (1937). It was renovated in 1988 by Trout Architects and Mark Mack, and CSHQA added a sculpture court and garden in 1997 and 1998, bringing it to 34,800 square feet (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Boise Art Museum: mixed private and public: foundations, individuals, business partners, and Idaho and federal arts grants

name: Bronx Museum of the Arts
overview: Contemporary art museum at 1040 Grand Concourse in the Bronx, New York.
Opened on 11 May 1971 in the Bronx County Courthouse rotunda, in a partnership between the Bronx Council on the Arts and the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Wikipedia credits Irma Fleck with founding it.
Moved in 1983 into a former synagogue the city bought in 1982. A $19 million Arquitectonica expansion opened in 2006 (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Bronx Museum of the Arts: mixed public, foundation and corporate funding: New York City and State arts agencies, federal grants, and named foundations and companies

Eddie Small, "Bronx Arts Museum Loses 6 Board Members in a Week" (29 August 2016)

name: Wave Hill
overview: Public garden and cultural center on a 28-acre site on a ridge above the Hudson River in Riverdale, the Bronx (Wave Hill, Wikipedia).

Founded as a public garden in 1965 (Wave Hill). The Perkins-Freeman family deeded the estate to the City of New York in 1960, at the suggestion of Robert Moses (Wikipedia). Wave Hill is one of New York City's 39 city-owned cultural institutions (Wave Hill FY2025 annual report). Wave Hill Incorporated is a 501(c)(3) charity with tax exemption dated June 1965 (ProPublica).
Named for the estate. Its earlier name was Perkins Garden, until Parks Commissioner Henry Stern renamed it Wave Hill in 1987 (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Wave Hill: city-owned site run by a nonprofit funded by government support, contributions and grants, investment income and earned income

name: Gibbes Museum of Art
overview: Art museum at 135 Meeting Street, Charleston, in a Beaux Arts building that opened on 11 April 1905 (Wikipedia).
Run by the Carolina Art Association, founded in 1858. The museum was formerly the Gibbes Art Gallery (Wikipedia).

Named for James Shoolbred Gibbes, who left $100,000 for "erection of a suitable building for the exhibitions of paintings". Relatives contested the will, the New York Supreme Court upheld the gift in December 1901 and the association received the money in 1903 (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Gibbes Museum of Art: contribution-funded: contributions were 84.2% of fiscal 2025 revenue, with rental and earned income

name: Columbus Museum of Art
overview: Art museum at 480 East Broad Street in downtown Columbus, Ohio, with a second site, CMA at The Pizzuti, at 632 Park Street in the Short North Arts District.

Founded in 1878 as the Columbus Gallery of Fine Arts, the first art museum in Ohio to receive a state charter. Renamed the Columbus Museum of Art in 1978 (Wikipedia). Brooke A. Minto is Executive Director and CEO.
Merged with the Columbus Art School in 1887. The school later became the Columbus College of Art & Design, and the two separated in 1987.
funding_verdict: Columbus Museum of Art: donor-funded: Columbus Foundation funds, Walter Foundation, Art Bridges Foundation, Battelle and JPMorgan Chase

name: Corning Museum of Glass
overview: Museum of glass art and history in Corning, New York.

Created in 1951 as the Corning Glass Center by Corning Glass Works for the company's 100th anniversary. Thomas S. Buechner was the founding director (Wikipedia). Corning Glass Works was renamed Corning Incorporated in 1989 (Wikipedia).

Building: Harrison & Abramovitz designed the original 1951 building. Gunnar Birkerts designed an addition that opened on 28 May 1980. Thomas Phifer redesigned the 2012 expansion, and the Contemporary Art + Design Wing opened on 20 March 2015 (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Corning Museum of Glass: founded by Corning Glass Works; Corning Incorporated is its major benefactor
wider_context: ProPublica and Investigative Post (Charlotte Keith and Masako Melissa Hirsch, "Corning's Glass Brimming With Taxpayer Subsidies", 27 March 2017) reported that Corning Incorporated was awarded $113 million in state and local subsidies between 2009 and 2015, according to an analysis by Investigative Post, ProPublica and the Columbia University Graduate School of Journalism. G. Thomas Tranter Jr., president of Corning's economic development arm, said the figure "far exceeds reality".

The article reported roughly $85 million in incentives for a 2013 factory expansion in Erwin, about $340,000 per job, and a $590,000 cost to the city of Corning from property tax breaks between 2009 and 2014, according to state reports.
Corning Incorporated is the museum's founder and, per Urban Glass in 2016, its major benefactor, and the same article names the museum among the winners of $4.8 million in grants.
